results.content: # Port of Savannah cruises to strong August; tariff impacts still seen at Port of Brunswick * The Port of Savannah saw a 9% year-over-year increase in cargo volume in August, marking its third-busiest month ever. * While Savannah's container volumes have grown, the Port of Brunswick's auto and machinery cargo has declined due to tariffs. The Port of Savannah continued another month of healthy container volumes in August, logging a 9% year-over-year increase in cargo, GPA officials announced at a board meeting Tuesday. The volumes marked the third busiest month in Georgia Ports Authority history even as uncertainty around tariffs have persisted throughout the calendar year. (The year) is better than expected,” said GPA President and CEO Griff Lynch. The Port of Savannah logged its second-busiest fiscal year on record at its close on June 30. The growth was anchored by record months in February, March and April due to customers frontloading cargo in anticipation of tariffs. June finally saw a tariff-related dip in cargo, but the start of this fiscal year has been strong. “I think consumption is better than expected, and that's a good thing." But while the Port of Savannah has remained resilient to volatility in global trade, the Port of Brunswick has been a different story. Brunswick’s port is the home of GPA’s Roll-On/Roll-Off operations, built to move motor vehicles and heavy machinery. Autos and machinery out of Bunswick’s Colonel’s Island terminal are down nearly 12% fiscal year to date, and down 14% year-over-year in August. For container outlook, the final quarter of the calendar year is typically a slower time for cargo, and Lynch predicted some moderation in coming months. The prospects of Imelda came roughly one year after Hurricane Helen ravaged Coastal Georgia and halted port operations. As of Tuesday morning, port operations were active and Lynch was not expecting any major disruptions to shipments. "Had Imelda taken a different track, we would have had some disruption, and we won't have that now." Tuesday was also a major meeting for GPA’s future growth. The Georgia Ports's approach is to have it when it's needed," said GPA Board Chairman Alec Poitevint.

results.title: Frontloading: The Double-Edged Sword of Global Shipping
results.content: HomeBusiness21st Century ChallengesFrontloading: The Double-Edged Sword of Global Shipping Business21st Century ChallengesGlobal TradeMaritimeContainer ShipsPortsRegulationsShippingSupply Chains # Frontloading: The Double-Edged Sword of Global Shipping As trade regulations continue to evolve – not to mention the uncertainty regarding tariffs, frontloading has become even more of an important strategy for U.S. exporters. #### **What Is Frontloading?** Frontloading is accelerating shipments to get around expected disruptions, or regulatory changes such as tariff deadlines (like the U.S.-China and U.S.-E.U. tariffs), labor strikes (like the ILA-USMX port negotiations), and seasonal demand spikes (like the dry season in the Amazon river). By rushing cargo through ports before risks materialize, shippers and importers aim to secure inventory and avoid any extra costs. #### **Benefits of Frontloading** For U.S. exporters and importers, frontloading is a strategic approach to mitigate the financial effects of a potential tariff or change. Importers may also reduce the risk of delays and extra costs associated with port congestion or tariffs by securing inventory early. Concentrating cargo flows into narrower windows leads to volume surges at major ports, as most recently seen in 2025 when E.U. importers accelerated U.S. goods shipments ahead of a postponed tariff deadline, resulting in overbooked vessels in the transatlantic routes and increased dwell times at Rotterdam and Antwerp. Similarly, during and before the USMX-ILA negotiations, to avoid the unrest and related charges, shippers rushed cargo and diverted some of the volume to U.S. West Coast ports, causing congestion and delays on both U.S. East Coast and U.S. West Coast ports. #### **How to Avoid Risks from Frontloading?** Congestion and frontloading may form a vicious cycle, but proactive planning can help exporters and importers turn these challenges into advantages. Title: China imports surge ahead of tariff deadlines | AJOT.COM
# China imports surge ahead of tariff deadlines. China imports surged in July, according to the August Global Shipping Report from Descartes Systems Group, showing imports from China increasing to 923,075 TEUs last month — a 44.4% month-over-month increase and the highest level in 2025 since January. The Descartes report also found that China imports surged in July 2025 across the top 10 US ports, increasing by 262,126 TEUs overall — a 42.9% month-over-month increase. “The July recovery reflects a combination of seasonal demand and suspected frontloading in response to the 30% temporary tariff rate on Chinese imports set to expire in mid-October.”. With respect to China imports, the two dates looming right now are the repeal of the de minimis exemption scheduled for August 29 – impacting all countries, not just China – and the expected October 15 end of the tariff truce between the US and China that temporarily brought rates down from the staggering peak of 145% to a more reasonable 30%. The Descartes report speculates that the July surge in Chinese volumes could be driven by shippers trying to import products before these deadlines, stocking up early for the holiday season to bypass the tariffs. “Frontloading is likely a factor,” confirms Jackson Wood, Director of Industry Strategy, Global Trade Intelligence for Descartes, “and we have anecdotal evidence – some companies have stated publicly that they have pulled forward their inventory to get ahead of new tariffs.”. “While July’s spike may reflect pre-tariff frontloading and temporary policy reprieves, it likely represents a high-water mark rather than a sustained trend, as looming tariff expirations and slowing demand point to potential declines in the months ahead,” the report continues. “The U.S. was very aggressive in the early stages of the negotiation with China but look at how quickly the Chinese throttling of some key exports – rare earth magnets and critical minerals – caused the US to reconsider its overall approach.”. I think companies are coming to the realization that the worst-case scenario of exceptionally high tariffs on Chinese imports is unlikely to come to pass – which is good news for shippers.”.

results.title: Race Against Tariff Deadlines: China–US Freight Rates Soar as Peak Season Begins Early
results.content:
Title: Race Against Tariff Deadlines: China–US Freight Rates Soar as Peak Season Begins Early
# Race Against Tariff Deadlines: China–US Freight Rates Soar as Peak Season Begins Early. The May-25 US–China tariff rollback triggered a sharp rebound in China–US ocean freight demand, pushing transpacific shipping rates significantly higher and marking an early start to the peak season. Importers are frontloading ahead of upcoming tariff deadlines in Jul-25 and Aug-25, while lingering port backlogs, vessel repositioning delays, and congestion in Asia are tightening capacity and fueling further rate hikes. Although US ports are preparing for increased volumes, Jun-25 and Jul-25 shipments are expected to remain below 2024 levels due to earlier frontloading and cautious ordering. Rising rates on other routes, like C/EA–Med and Europe–South America WC, reflect broader geopolitical and trade shifts. The tariff truce may also support longer-term agricultural trade ties between the US and China. ## Tariff Rollback Sparks China–US Freight Rebound, Driving Up Rates Ahead of Early Peak Season. The truce reached between the United States (US) and China in May-25, which included a mutual rollback of reciprocal tariffs by 115% for a 90-day period starting May 14, 2025, triggered a sharp rebound in ocean freight demand on the China–US route. As trade activity picked up, freight rates rose, with the Freightos Baltic Index climbing 3.8% month-on-month (MoM) to USD 2,123.76 per 40-foot container. The shipping demand recovery reflects the substantial relief provided by the tariff reductions since US import duties were lowered from 145% to 30%, while China’s tariffs dropped from 125% to 10%. For instance, Asia-US West Coast (WC) route prices rose from USD 2,395/40-foot container in the week ending May 13 to USD 2,788/40-foot container by the week ending May 27, representing a 16.41% rise. Similarly, on the Asia–US East Coast (EC) route, freight rates grew from USD 3,406 in the week ending May 13 to USD 4,223 by May 27. The sharp rise in transpacific container rates signals the early onset of the peak shipping season, driven largely by frontloading efforts ahead of key tariff deadlines. Despite the rebound in demand, China’s ports are still likely working through a backlog of goods that accumulated during the Apr-25–May-25 slowdown in China–US trade.

results.content:
Title: Retailers to continue frontloading amid tariff tumult: forecast - Logfret
# Retailers to continue frontloading amid tariff tumult: forecast. Retailers to continue frontloading amid tariff tumult: forecast. **A sustained cargo surge at U.S. ports will continue as Trump administration policy uncertainty continues, per the National Retail Federation and Hackett Associates’ Global Port Tracker.**. The U.S. President has already increased import taxes on goods from China by 20% while promising a start of reciprocal tariffs on April 2. These actions are the primary drivers of the frontloading by shippers, according to NRF, even amid last week’s back-and-forth on duties for Canada and Mexico imports. “The on-again, off-again tariffs against Canada and Mexico won’t have a direct impact on port volumes because most of those goods move by truck or rail,” NRF said. Last Tuesday, the U.S. President lifted a monthlong pause on the 25% tariffs directed at Canada and Mexico he announced in February and subsequently delayed the implementation of the duties for goods compliant with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement two days later. Beyond tariffs, another Trump administration initiative could alter import volumes at U.S. ports, according to the report. In February, the United States Trade Representative proposed the implementation of fees of up to $1.5 million for ships built in China docking at U.S. ports. “Given that a significant portion of the global container fleet has been built in China, this means that there will be further costs that will be passed on to cargo owners and ultimately the consumer,” the founder of Hackett Associates said in the release. Should the USTR’s proposal be implemented, it could lead to increased use of larger vessels and shipment consolidation to avoid making multiple ports calls in the U.S., potentially reducing activity at smaller ports. “Ports accommodated the surge in import volume in the final quarter of 2024 without major issues, but this will place additional pressure on the supply chain while also harming the nation’s smaller ports,” Hackett said. Although imports are expected to increase in the near term, volumes are expected to decline for the first time since September 2023 in June and July. However, the decrease would be partially due to frontloading ahead of last fall’s East and Gulf Coast port strike, per the release. ## Post navigation. ### Related posts.
